evidence.label: Finite Smith–Toda Complexes at Varying Primes
A finite Smith–Toda complex V(4) at the prime 1009

headline: Claims Smith–Toda complexes exist at every height if the prime may grow, with an explicit V(4) at the prime 1009.
scope: Two linked papers: an existence result for every height at some prime depending on the height, and one explicit case.
plain: A Smith–Toda complex V(n) is a finite building block of stable homotopy theory that kills the first n+1 chromatic numbers once each. Classical work built V(1), V(2) and V(3) at large enough primes. V(4) was recorded as open at every prime. One paper claims V(n) exists for every n at some prime chosen for that n. A second paper claims an explicit V(4) at the prime 1009.
doesNot: This does not show that one prime works at every height, and it does not give a bound on the prime in general.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Larry Smith, realizing complex bordism modules; with Adams and Toda, the first complexes V(1) to V(3)
scorecard.significanceWhy: It claims a classical realization problem in stable homotopy theory at every height, where earlier constructions stopped at V(3).

explanation:
Start with the whole numbers and divide out by a prime p. The result is the numbers mod p. Topology has a version of this step for spectra, the basic objects of stable homotopy theory. At height zero the Moore spectrum kills p this way[12]. Brown–Peterson homology, written BP, assigns to each spectrum a list of algebraic data. For the sphere it is a polynomial ring in numbers v₁, v₂, v₃ and so on. The number vᵢ sits in degree 2(pⁱ − 1). At p = 1009, v₁ sits in degree 2,016. The number v₄ sits in degree 2,072,977,845,120.

A Smith–Toda complex V(n) is a finite spectrum whose BP homology kills p, v₁, up to vₙ, each once. Killing the next number needs an actual map of spectra that multiplies by it. Algebra describes the result once that map exists, but it does not supply the map[3]. That is the obstacle. Adams, Smith and Toda built V(1), V(2) and V(3) when p is larger than 2, 4 and 6[13]. Hopkins and Smith could kill higher powers of these numbers at every height[8]. But the question asks for first powers. A 2023 version of a paper by Culver and Zhang recorded V(4) as open at every prime[4]. Nave proved that V((p+1)/2) does not exist for p at least 7[5]. At p = 7 that rules out V(4), since (7 + 1)/2 = 4. At p = 1009 the barrier is V(505), far above height four.

The first paper claims that V(n) exists for every n, at a prime p that depends on n[1]. It works with an ultraproduct, a way to average a statement over all primes at once. The ultraproduct is formed from ordinary p-local spectra[6]. Only finitely many maps then need to come down to one actual prime[7]. The result names no bound on the prime and no single prime for all heights[2].

The second paper claims an explicit V(4) at p = 1009[9]. It builds V(3) with a product, then shows that v₄ survives a spectral sequence, a step-by-step calculation of maps[11]. The large prime keeps the finite inequalities in the calculation comfortable[10].

How sure is this? There is no Lean check. A computer proof checker has not looked at any part of it. Both papers rely on long algebraic calculations and delicate constructions in stable homotopy theory. No specialist review of either paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the proofs hold. The all-height result allows the prime to grow and gives no bound. There is no Lean check and no published specialist review.

glossary.meaning: The basic object of stable homotopy theory, a stabilized version of a space.
An invariant that turns a spectrum into algebraic data over a polynomial ring in numbers v₁, v₂ and so on.
A finite spectrum whose BP homology kills p and v₁ up to vₙ, each to the first power.
The spectrum version of the numbers mod p, which is V(0).
The index n that says how many of the numbers v₁, v₂ and so on are killed.
A way to combine one object for each prime into a single object that averages over all primes.
A step-by-step calculation that approximates an answer page by page.
